elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang for cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies up to March 16, 2023, to conduct a meta-analysis of global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a meta-analysis (a form of systematic review), and the title also states 'systematic review and meta-analysis'.

elements.quote: However, the trend of reinfection rate over time is not clear. ... to conduct a meta-analysis of global SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate.
elements.reason: The objective is implied through the background gap and the stated purpose of the meta-analysis, but there is no explicit objective/review question statement in the abstract.

elements.quote: We searched ... for cohort studies, case-control studies, and cross-sectional studies up to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The abstract specifies eligible study designs but does not state other key inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., reinfection definition, minimum sample size, exclusions).

elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang ... up to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The abstract lists all information sources and the date of the last search.

elements.quote: The risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool.
elements.reason: The abstract names the specific risk-of-bias assessment tools used.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed for age, country, study type, and study population, and time-varying reinfection rates of SARS-CoV-2 were estimated using meta-regression.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis methods: meta-analysis, subgroup analyses, and meta-regression.

elements.quote: A total of 55 studies involving 111,846 cases of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection were included.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies and participants, with relevant characteristics (subgroups by age, country, study type, population) summarized.

elements.quote: The pooled SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate was 0.94% (95% CI : 0.65 -1.35%). In the subgroup analyses, there were statistically significant differences in the pooled reinfection rates by reinfection variant, and study type (P < 0.05).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcome (pooled reinfection rate) and subgroup findings.

elements.quote: The pooled SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate was 0.94% (95% CI : 0.65 -1.35%).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports the summary estimate with its 95% confidence interval.

elements.quote: SARS-CoV-2 is at risk of reinfection and the Omicron variant has a higher reinfection rate than other currently known variants.
elements.reason: For subgroup comparisons, the abstract indicates the direction of effect, identifying Omicron as having a higher reinfection rate than other variants.
The abstract contains no statement of limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision); limitations appear only in the main text.

elements.quote: The results of this study could help guide public health measures and vaccination strategies in response to the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
elements.reason: The conclusion provides an interpretation of the time-varying reinfection pattern and its implications for public health and vaccination strategies.
The abstract does not mention funding; funding information appears only in the Funding section (text_19).
The abstract does not report the registry name or registration number; PROSPERO registration (CRD42023411778) appears only in the Study Design section (text_6).

elements.quote: There is a significant increase in the number of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection reports in various countries. However, the trend of reinfection rate over time is not clear.
elements.reason: The abstract background describes the current state of knowledge (increasing reinfection reports) and explicitly identifies the key uncertainty (unclear trend of reinfection rate over time); the Introduction (text_4) further describes the global burden and ongoing mutation of SARS-CoV-2.

elements.quote: The results of this study could help guide public health measures and vaccination strategies in response to the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic.
elements.reason: The need for the review is explained: resolving the unclear time trend of reinfection is framed as important for guiding public health measures and vaccination strategies, and the Introduction (text_4) establishes SARS-CoV-2 as a continuing global health threat.

elements.quote: the advantage of this study was that compared with the previous meta-analysis of the SARSCoV-2 reinfection rate, first, to avoid the heterogeneous impact of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection definition on SARSCoV-2 reinfection rates...
elements.reason: The Discussion acknowledges previous meta-analyses of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate and explains how the current review improves on them, but the previous review is not identified or cited, and this comparison is not presented in the Introduction as part of the rationale.
This is a review of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rates (etiology/prognosis), not a review of intervention effects, so no mechanism of action needs to be described.
This review does not evaluate complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: Therefore, the aim of this study was to conduct a meta-analysis to describe and summarize the current reinfection rates in different regions and among diverse populations. Furthermore, the study sought to examine trends in reinfection rates over time, so as to provide reference for the development of global unified reinfection standards and reinfection measures in the future.
elements.reason: The review objectives are explicitly stated: to summarize current SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rates across regions/populations and to examine time trends in reinfection rates. The objectives are clearly articulated, though not framed in a formal named framework.
This is a review estimating the frequency (rate) of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection, not a review of intervention effects, so planned PICO-style intervention comparisons do not apply.

elements.quote: The inclusion criteria were: (1) Conformed to research questions, i.e., studies that estimated the reinfection rate of SARS-CoV-2 or we could calculate it based on the data provided in the paper; (2) The study design included cohort study, case-control study, and descriptive study; (3) The study fited our working definition of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection... The exclusion criteria were: (1) The sample size was less than 20; (2) Belonged to one of the following types of studies: editorial, case report, case series study, systematic review, meta-analysis, animal experiment, news report
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria are explicitly listed, including the review question (reinfection rate estimation), eligible study designs, the working definition of reinfection (positive result at least 90 days after primary infection), and exclusion criteria such as minimum sample size and publication types.

elements.quote: To avoid language bias, the search was not limited to any language... (4) Grey literature, including a range of documents not controlled by commercial publishing organizations.
elements.reason: Language and publication status (grey literature exclusion) are specified, but no dissemination year restriction or other report characteristics are reported.

elements.quote: One of them reported only the reinfection rate, but not the associated number of first infections as well as the number of reinfections... Therefore, we excluded the above literature with the number of unreported infections
elements.reason: The review excludes studies lacking necessary data but does not distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed by meta-regression to fit stratified rates of reinfection based on variables such as variant and country, and we also used spline regression to fit time-varying reinfection rates
elements.reason: Synthesis groups are specified (age, variant, country, study population, study type per Table 1) and linked to the objectives of summarizing reinfection rates in different regions and diverse populations and examining time trends.

elements.quote: In order to avoid data heterogeneity in metaanalysis while ensuring data quantity, we used previous literature and previous definitions of reinfection in some countries as the criteria for included literature
elements.reason: A rationale is given for the 90-day reinfection definition restriction (based on WHO/CDC advice and reducing heterogeneity), but rationales for other restrictions such as the minimum sample size of 20 or grey literature exclusion are not provided.

elements.quote: A meta-regression analysis was conducted on literature reporting cases of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection globally to estimate the incidence of reinfection of SARS-CoV-2 (as of March 16, 2023)
elements.reason: The last search date is reported as March 16, 2023, consistent with the search window ending on that date.

elements.quote: We searched for papers published on PubMed, Web of Science, Medline(Ovid), Embase(Ovid), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure(CNKI), Wanfang using ... from January 1, 2020 to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: All seven databases are named, platforms specified for Ovid databases, and the coverage/search date range (January 1, 2020 to March 16, 2023) is given.

elements.quote: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure(CNKI), Wanfang ... from January 1, 2020 to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials is named as a searched register, with the same date restrictions applied to all sources.
No websites or search engines were reported as searched; only bibliographic databases and registers were used.
No organisations or manufacturers were reported as contacted to identify studies.
No individuals were reported as contacted to identify studies.
No reference list screening was reported; grey literature was explicitly excluded.
No backward or forward citation searching was reported in the methods.
No journals or conference proceedings were consulted directly as sources.

elements.quote: We searched for papers published on PubMed, Web of Science, Medline(Ovid), Embase(Ovid), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure(CNKI), Wanfang using 'COVID-19' , '2019-nCoV' , 'SARS-COV-2' , 'Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2' , 'reinfection' , 'recurrence' , 'repeat positive' and 'repeat infections' as keywords, from January 1, 2020 to March 16, 2023 (Additional file 2).
elements.reason: Databases, keywords, and date range are reported, and the full search strategy is deferred to Additional file 2 (confirmed as 'Search strategy' in the supplementary list); however, the complete search strings as actually run (e.g., Boolean combinations, field tags) are not shown in the main text.

elements.quote: from January 1, 2020 to March 16, 2023
elements.reason: The date limit is stated and implicitly tied to the review's data cutoff (as of March 16, 2023), and text_7 states 'the search was not limited to any language' to avoid language bias; but other potential limits/filters are not explicitly described or justified against eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: The search strategy we used was based on previous studies
elements.reason: The authors state the search strategy was based on previous studies, but the specific published search approaches or filters are not cited and any adaptations are not described.
No evidence that natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were used to identify or refine search terms.
No evidence that tools were used to translate search strings between sources; the same keywords were reported across databases.
No validation of the search strategy is reported in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) is reported in the retrieved evidence.
The search used standard concept keywords (COVID-19 and reinfection terms) consistent with a PICO-like structure; no evidence indicates a non-PICO conceptual structure requiring description.

elements.quote: The reviewers independently (CY, Z-WH, H-XY, C-MS, LX, H-HP) screened the literature based on inclusion and exclusion criteria.
elements.reason: Six reviewers are named for screening, but the number of reviewers is not specified separately for each screening stage (title/abstract vs full-text eligibility).

elements.quote: The reviewers independently (CY, Z-WH, H-XY, C-MS, LX, H-HP) screened the literature based on inclusion and exclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that reviewers screened independently.

elements.quote: Conflicts were resolved by other independent reviewers (ZT Y-CH).
elements.reason: Disagreement resolution is described: conflicts were resolved by other independent reviewers.
No process for obtaining or confirming eligibility information from study investigators is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: if the included article was neither in English nor in Chinese and did not provide an English abstract or full text, we used an online translator (Google Translate) for translation.
elements.reason: Methods for translating non-English articles for eligibility assessment are reported (Google Translate).
No automation tools are reported as being used in the selection process; screening was performed manually by named reviewers.
No externally derived classifiers were used in the study selection process.
No internally derived classifiers were used in the study selection process.
No machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping rules were used in screening.
No crowdsourcing platforms were used in study selection.
No previously screened datasets were used to eliminate records; all records were screened from the authors' own database searches.
The manuscript states that reviewers independently screened the literature and performed risk of bias assessment, but it never specifies how many reviewers collected/extracted data from each report.

Independence is reported for screening ('The reviewers independently (CY, Z-WH, H-XY, C-MS, LX, H-HP) screened the literature') and risk of bias assessment, but not for the data extraction/collection process itself.
Conflict resolution is described only for screening ('Conflicts were resolved by other independent reviewers (ZT Y-CH)') and risk of bias, not for disagreements during data collection/extraction.
No process for obtaining or confirming data from study investigators is reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.
No automation tools used for data collection are described; only R statistical software is mentioned, for analysis, not data extraction.

elements.quote: if the included article was neither in English nor in Chinese and did not provide an English abstract or full text, we used an online translator (Google Translate) for translation.
elements.reason: The methods for translating non-English articles during the review process are explicitly reported.
No software for extracting data from figures is mentioned in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: If the paper did not mention the reinfection variant, we classified the reinfection variants based on the WHO standards according to the study period.
elements.reason: A decision rule for handling missing reinfection variant data is given, and text_8 notes selecting one of two articles on the same population, but no general rule for choosing among multiple reports of the same study or resolving inconsistencies in extracted data is fully described.

elements.quote: The complete information extracted included the first author, study period, country, study population, sample size, study design, reinfected variants, time between two positive tests (days), age, reinfection rate, and the number of reinfections.
elements.reason: The outcome (SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rate) is defined via a working definition (positive lab result at least 90 days after primary infection), and extracted data items are listed, but outcome domains are not systematically listed and defined as outcome domains per se.

elements.quote: time between two positive tests (days)
elements.reason: Time between two positive tests was extracted and used in meta-regression for time-varying rates, but an explicit time frame of measurement for each outcome domain is not fully specified.
No statement on whether all compatible results (all measures, time points, analyses) within each outcome domain were sought.
Conditional; since it is not stated that only a subset of compatible results was sought, no selection process needs describing.
No evidence of changes to outcome definitions during the review is reported.
No evidence of changes to result-selection processes is reported.
No explicit statement of which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions with rationale for prioritisation.

elements.quote: The complete information extracted included the first author, study period, country, study population, sample size, study design, reinfected variants, time between two positive tests (days), age, reinfection rate, and the number of reinfections.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists all variables for which data were sought during extraction.

elements.quote: If the paper did not mention the reinfection variant, we classified the reinfection variants based on the WHO standards according to the study period.
elements.reason: The authors describe an assumption/handling rule for missing or unclear information (unreported reinfection variant).
No tool or guidance used to determine which data items to collect is cited anywhere in the retrieved evidence; only the extraction form (Additional file 3) is referenced.

elements.quote: We used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) to evaluate the literature quality of cohort and case-control studies, and the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tool (JBI) for cross-sectional studies (Additional file 4).
elements.reason: Both risk-of-bias tools (NOS and JBI) are named and matched to study designs.

elements.quote: When the star rating in NOS was less than 3, or the number of 'yes' in JBI was less than 5 [23], we categorized the paper as 'high risk of bias'.
elements.reason: Scoring elements (stars, 'yes' items) are implied, but the specific domains/items of NOS and JBI are not described in the retrieved text; details may be in Additional file 4, which is not shown.

elements.quote: When the star rating in NOS was less than 3, or the number of 'yes' in JBI was less than 5 [23], we categorized the paper as 'high risk of bias'.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias categorization ('high risk of bias') is reported with explicit rules for deriving it.
No adaptations to the NOS or JBI tools are described in the retrieved evidence.
Only existing tools (NOS, JBI) were used; no newly developed tool is reported.

elements.quote: Risk bias assessment was performed by two independent reviewers (H-XY, C-MS), and inconsistencies were judged by other independent reviewers (CY, Z-WH).
elements.reason: Number of reviewers (two), independence, and disagreement-resolution by other independent reviewers are reported.
No processes for obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators are described.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment are mentioned; manual assessment by reviewers is reported.

elements.quote: We used meta-analysis to evaluate the pooled rate of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection in the included studies... we converted the reinfection rate to an approximate normal distribution. Four transformations were taken: log transformation, logit transformation, arcsine transformation, and double arcsine transformation. Through the hypothesis test after the transformation, we decided to use the logit transformation
elements.reason: The effect measure for the single outcome (reinfection rate/proportion, presented with 95% CIs) is specified, including the logit transformation used for pooling.
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting the size of the reinfection rate effect are reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.

The review synthesizes a single outcome (reinfection rate) as a proportion; there is no indication that any synthesized results were re-expressed using a different effect measure, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: However, when the rate is close to 0 or 1, two problems will occur in the meta-regression: the confidence interval may exceed the interval of 0-1, and the variance is squeezed towards 0. Therefore, we converted the reinfection rate to an approximate normal distribution... Through the hypothesis test after the transformation, we decided to use the logit transformation
elements.reason: The choice of the logit transformation is justified statistically, but the underlying choice of rate/proportion as the effect measure itself is not explicitly justified beyond it being the study question.

elements.quote: The inclusion criteria were: (1) Conformed to research questions, i.e., studies that estimated the reinfection rate of SARS-CoV-2 or we could calculate it based on the data provided in the paper; (2) The study design included cohort study, case-control study, and descriptive study; (3) The study fited our working definition of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection... The complete information extracted included the first author, study period, country, study population, sample size, study design, reinfected variants, time between two positive tests (days), age, reinfection rate, and the number of reinfections.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes general inclusion/exclusion criteria and data extraction of characteristics (variant, country, age, study type) later used in subgroup analyses and meta-regression, and text_8 notes studies were excluded from the meta-analysis when required data (number of first infections/reinfections) were unreported. However, there is no explicit description of the process used to decide which studies were eligible for each planned synthesis (e.g., tabulating study characteristics against planned synthesis groups), so the reporting is only partial.

elements.quote: Therefore, we converted the reinfection rate to an approximate normal distribution. Four transformations were taken: log transformation, logit transformation, arcsine transformation, and double arcsine transformation. Through the hypothesis test after the transformation, we decided to use the logit transformation (see Additional file 5 for specific results).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes data preparation for synthesis, including conversion of reinfection rates via four transformations and selection of logit transformation. Additional data handling (e.g., classifying variants by WHO standards when not reported, calculating rates from provided data) is also described in text_7.

No methods text describes the tabular structures used to display results. Table 1 appears in results ('Table 1 Results of subgroup analysis') but the methods section does not describe how tables were constructed or what data they include.

elements.quote: Subgroup analysis was also performed to obtain reinfection rates and forest plots according to age, variant, and country.
elements.reason: The methods mention producing forest plots, and results reference forest plots in Additional file 6 and meta-regression figures (e.g., Fig. 5), but there is no systematic description of all graphical display methods (e.g., meta-regression plots, funnel plots) in the methods.

No statement reports the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs; subgroup groupings (age, variant, country) are reported as analyses but not as an ordering/grouping scheme for displays.
Only standard displays (forest plots, subgroup tables, meta-regression plots) are indicated; no non-standard graphs are reported, so no rationale is required.

elements.quote: All analyses were performed using R statistical software (version 4.2.3).
elements.reason: Software and version number used for the statistical synthesis are explicitly reported.
A meta-analysis was performed, so no alternative synthesis method needed to be described.

elements.quote: If heterogeneity was low, a fixed-effects model was used to combine rates and correction estimates from different studies. Otherwise, a random-effects model was used.
elements.reason: The choice of fixed- vs random-effects model is reported with its rationale (level of heterogeneity).

elements.quote: Therefore, we converted the reinfection rate to an approximate normal distribution. Four transformations were taken: log transformation, logit transformation, arcsine transformation, and double arcsine transformation. Through the hypothesis test after the transformation, we decided to use the logit transformation
elements.reason: The statistical method for pooling rates (logit transformation of proportions) is described, along with meta-regression and subgroup analysis methods.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity between studies was expressed using Cochran's Q statistic test ( P < 0.05) as well as I 2 > 50%.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify heterogeneity (Cochran's Q and I-squared with thresholds) are reported.
A random-effects model was used, but the between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) is not reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.
The method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect in the random-effects meta-analysis is not reported.
No other random-effects implementation details (e.g., exact R packages/functions, tau-squared handling) are reported beyond the model choice itself.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed; frequentist methods (meta-analysis, meta-regression in R) were used.

No methods for handling statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study are described; the only related note is exclusion of duplicate-population studies at screening (text_8), not a synthesis-level dependency method.

elements.quote: due to the lack of specific data in the included literature, subgroup analysis of disease severity and vaccination could not be carried out, so it was impossible to explore all the sources of heterogeneity of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection rates.
elements.reason: Planned subgroup syntheses (disease severity, vaccination) that could not be performed are identified with the reason (lack of specific data), albeit reported in the limitations rather than methods.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed by meta-regression to fit stratified rates of reinfection based on variables such as variant and country, and we also used spline regression to fit time-varying reinfection rates that did not account for heterogeneity.
elements.reason: Methods to explore heterogeneity (subgroup analysis via meta-regression, spline regression) are explicitly described in the Methods section.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed for age, reinfection variant, country, study population, and study type respectively
elements.reason: Factors and their levels (e.g., variants Wild/Alpha/Delta/Omicron; countries; age >=18/<18) are reported, but no expected direction of effect modification is stated anywhere.
The manuscript does not state whether heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.

elements.quote: | Reinfected variants    |                  |              |                  |        | 0.0016   |
elements.reason: Table 1 reports P values for differences between subgroups and the text notes statistically significant differences, but the statistical method used to compare subgroup effects is not described in the Methods.
Meta-analysis was suitable and performed for all included data; no informal (non-statistical) exploration of heterogeneity was used, so this requirement does not apply.
The manuscript does not identify which heterogeneity analyses were post hoc versus pre-specified.

elements.quote: we used two methods for sensitivity analysis: the first method involved recalculating the combined values by excluding highly biased papers and comparing the differences in results before and after exclusion; the second method involved sequentially excluding each included paper and analyzing whether there were significant differences in results before and after exclusion.
elements.reason: The methods describe two sensitivity analyses (excluding high risk-of-bias studies; leave-one-out), and results are reported in text_13 with details in Additional file 8.
No evidence indicates whether the sensitivity analyses were pre-specified or identifies any as not pre-specified.

No methods for assessing risk of bias due to missing results (reporting biases), such as funnel plots or Egger tests, are described anywhere in the retrieved evidence. The limitations section even notes that 'the pattern of publication bias in the field of single-arm study with single-group rate is not clear, and funnel plot analysis may lead to inaccurate conclusions,' but no assessment method was reported as used.
